conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Name], a clinician who specializes in helping new mothers navigate the emotional ups and downs that can come after childbirth. Today I’d like to use a short, well-studied tool called the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—EPDS for short—to get a quick picture of how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. It’s simply ten questions; there are no right or wrong answers, and everything you share stays between us unless you give permission otherwise or there’s an immediate safety concern. My goal is to create a safe, non-judgmental space where you can speak freely.

We’ll take it one question at a time, and you can answer in your own words—no need to worry about numbers or multiple-choice options. Ready to begin?

First, how have you been feeling overall in the past week—have you been able to enjoy things, or has enjoyment felt hard to come by?

Honestly, most things just feel kind of… flat. I used to look forward to little stuff—watching a show I liked, grabbing coffee with a friend—and now it’s like I go through the motions but don’t really feel it. I’ll still try, but the spark isn’t there. Even when I’m holding the baby and everyone’s saying, “Isn’t this the best?” I’m thinking, “Shouldn’t I be happier right now?”
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Sometimes I’ll catch myself chuckling—like when the baby makes those tiny sneezes or my husband tries to swaddle and ends up in a knot—but the laughter feels kind of distant, almost like I’m hearing it from outside myself. Most of the time I have to force it, and then I feel guilty because I think I should be enjoying these moments more.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

Not really. I’ll make plans—like meeting a friend for a walk or ordering my favorite take-out—and I keep hoping the excitement will kick in, but it doesn’t. When the time comes, I’m just tired and wondering if it’s worth the effort. Even little “good” things on the calendar feel more like chores than something to look forward to.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

All the time. If the baby spits up a lot, I assume it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing. If he’s fussy, I’m sure I’m not soothing him the way a “good mom” would. Last night he wouldn’t settle after a feeding and I lay there thinking, “I’m already failing him and he’s only three weeks old.” I know logically babies just cry, but my head keeps whispering it’s my fault.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yeah… pretty much every day. I’ll be folding laundry and suddenly my heart’s racing because I’m convinced the baby’s breathing sounds different, or I’ll worry that the formula isn’t the right temperature and he’ll get sick. Nothing has to trigger it—my mind just jumps to the worst-case scenario and I can’t shake the tight-chest feeling until I check on him again… and then I feel silly for overreacting.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Sometimes it hits out of nowhere—like yesterday, I was just rocking the baby in the nursery and suddenly felt this rush of dread, almost like something awful was about to happen. My hands got shaky, my heart was pounding, and I had to put him in the crib for a second just so I could sit down and breathe. There wasn’t any real reason; it just felt like panic rising up in my chest.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yeah… most days. I’ll start the morning thinking, “Okay, I just need to feed him, change him, maybe fold that basket of laundry,” and suddenly it feels like the list keeps growing and I’m drowning in it. Sometimes I look around at the bottles, the diapers, the mess, and I just want to sit on the floor and cry because it feels like too much to handle—even though I know it’s just normal baby stuff.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

It’s been rough at night. I’ll finally get him down, but then my head keeps circling through all the “what-ifs” and everything I think I did wrong that day. Even when I’m exhausted, I lie there staring at the ceiling or scrolling my phone, hoping the worries will quiet down long enough for me to drift off—then the baby stirs and the cycle starts over.
I have felt sad or miserable

Pretty much every day this week. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest that doesn’t really lift. I’ll look at the baby and feel like I should be glowing, but instead there’s just this dull ache. Some afternoons I just sit in the rocking chair with him asleep on me and tears slide down for no clear reason—I’m not even sure what I’m crying about half the time.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Yeah… it’s happened a few times. Yesterday I spilled a little pumped milk on the counter and just burst into tears—like, full-on sobbing. My husband found me wiping it up and kept saying, “It’s just a couple ounces, it’s okay,” but I couldn’t stop. I felt so stupid for crying over something small, but it was like the sadness just spilled out with the milk.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me
No—never. I feel low and overwhelmed, but I haven’t thought about hurting myself. I just want to feel better so I can be the mom my baby deserves.

You've shared that the past week has felt overwhelmingly heavy: joy seems distant, simple tasks feel like they're piling up beyond your control, and tears come easily over things that never used to bother you. Even when you try to enjoy your baby or plan pleasant moments, a persistent low mood and constant worries crowd them out, leaving you exhausted and blaming yourself for things you logically know aren't your fault.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 23, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports laughter is rare, distant, and forced; clear reduction from baseline enjoyment</sym>, <sym>Patient reports almost complete loss of anticipatory enjoyment; plans feel like chores and excitement never arrives.</sym>, <sym>Patient reports constant self-blame, interpreting normal infant behaviors as personal failures, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, unprovoked anxiety episodes with physical symptoms and intrusive catastrophic thoughts, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense dread and physical panic symptoms occurring "sometimes" with no clear trigger, matching the "Yes, sometimes" option.</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily overwhelm with growing tasks and emotional drowning, matching "sometimes I haven't been coping as well as usual"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes persistent, intrusive night-time worries that repeatedly prevent sleep despite exhaustion, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily pervasive sadness, physical heaviness, unexplained tearfulness, and emotional numbness, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports multiple crying episodes triggered by minor events, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** Your score of 23 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable <med>postpartum major depression</med>. You endorsed daily or almost-daily <sym>low mood</sym>, <sym>loss of interest</sym>, <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sup>, <sym>concentration problems</sym>, <sym>sleep disturbance</sym>, and <sym>appetite/appetite-related distress</sym>, matching core <med>DSM-5 criteria for Major Depressive Disorder with Peripartum Onset</med>. The additional <sym>free-floating anxiety</sym> and sudden <sym>panic symptoms</sym> suggest co-occurring <med>postpartum anxiety</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent evaluation with your <med>primary care provider</med> or <med>obstetrician</med> within the next few days
2. Ask about evidence-based treatments such as <med>CBT</med> or <med>IPT</med> and discuss whether an <med>antidepressant</med> is appropriate
3. Reach out today to a trusted adult who can help with infant care while you rest and attend appointments
4. Schedule a follow-up call with this office in 48 h to confirm appointment made and review any crisis resources
5. Keep basic needs simple: aim for one short outdoor walk, balanced snacks, and accept help with housework
6. Continue monitoring; if any thoughts of self-harm ever arise, treat as an emergency and call 911 or go to the nearest ED
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 23: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Summary  
Patient: 3-week postpartum mother  
Date: [today]

Presenting concerns endorsed on 10-item EPDS-type questionnaire:

<sym>Depressive symptoms</sym>  
- Persistent low mood, “heavy” feeling daily  
- Marked anhedonia (minimal enjoyment, forced laughter)  
- Frequent crying spells with minimal precipitant (e.g., spilled milk)  
- Self-criticism & inappropriate guilt (“already failing him”)  

<sym>Anxiety symptoms</sym>  
- Daily free-floating worry, worst-case thinking  
- Episodic panic-like attacks (sudden dread, palpitations, shakiness)  
- Hypervigilance re infant safety  

<sym>Functional impact</sym>  
- Overwhelmed by routine tasks, “drowning” feeling  
- Sleep initiation impaired even when infant settled (rumination)  

Risk factors  
- Primiparous, 3 wk postpartum  
- Absence of bonding pleasure  
- No self-harm ideation endorsed (score 0)  

Screening impression  
Elevated depressive and anxiety symptoms consistent with probable <med>postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety</med>. No acute safety concerns identified today. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment and discussion of supports/interventions.
